author: Russell Brand
description:
When a Texas jury found Karmelo Anthony guilty of murdering 17-year-old Austin Metcalf at a high school track meet, the immediate outrage from protesters was not about the evidence — it was about the color of the jury. Russell Brand confronts the uncomfortable reality that 250 years of American judicial progress is being quietly dismantled the moment jury composition is treated as a racial headcount rather than a measure of truth and evidence. The Karmelo Anthony trial, racial bias in the justice system, and the politics of identity in American courts have collided into a crisis that Russell warns will only hand authoritarians the exact justification they have been waiting for. You cannot demand a colorblind society and simultaneously demand that justice be color-coded.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Keir Starmer stood up and delivered what sounded like the most carefully prepared answer about free speech anyone has ever given — free speech yes, incitement to violence no — and Russell Brand asked the only question that matters in response: who decides where that line is? The answer is the people in authority. The same people who have presided over a generation of milksop, anodyne, veal calf political leadership that has systematically hollowed out every institution it touched. Keir Starmer does not know the details of the case he is being asked about. He is not interested in the details. He is interested in sounding like someone who believes in free speech while quietly reserving the right to define exactly what that means. That is not free speech. That is managed speech. And the man delivering it is the most polished phony to ever stand at a British dispatch box.

description:
Look at the last decade of British political leadership — anodyne, milksop, veal calf figures, hopeless saps invested primarily in their own cultural class and not in the nation they were supposedly elected to serve. Keir Starmer polled at 9% approval. His deputy was fired over alleged tax cheating. Sadiq Khan spent ten years turning London into what Russell Brand describes as a no go zone. The political class on both sides of the Atlantic has been captured by the same priorities, the same donors, the same cultural allegiances, and the same contempt for the ordinary people they claim to represent. author: Russell Brand
description:
The people of Britain took to the streets chanting for Keir Starmer to go, and today he went. Starmer resigned in a televised statement after coming under mounting pressure from his own Labour Party, following Andy Burnham's decisive by-election win in Makerfield. Russell Brand asked the question months ago that nobody in Westminster wanted to answer — do the people of Britain actually feel represented with political integrity by this government? The agricultural protests, the cost of living crisis, the Epstein connections, the defence resignations, and finally the streets themselves gave the answer. This would make Starmer the seventh prime minister to leave office in a single decade — a rate of churn that tells you everything about a political class that has run out of ideas, out of credibility, and out of people willing to defend it. The question now is whether the next person through the door of Downing Street will be any different at all.
